title: Days, the poem
hook: in his poem Days, the days pass like silent gift-bearers and he takes only a few herbs

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emerson forgetting: the name gone, the love still there. Your line was gentleness stays. Did someone get your patient face? Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

A procession goes past a garden. Single file, no end to it. The walkers are barefoot and silent, wrapped up so you can't see their faces. Each one carries something. Some carry crowns. Some carry bundles of sticks for the fire. Each one stops in front of whoever is watching and offers a gift, whatever that person wants. A man sits in his garden and watches them go by. One stops in front of him. That's the scene of a short poem Emerson called Days. The walkers are the days themselves. And what the man in the garden picks is the reason the poem stings. Today's word is the poem's title.
screen: `A SILENT PROCESSION.` → `EACH ONE OFFERS A GIFT.` → `THE WALKERS ARE THE DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the disguise. The poem opens, "Daughters of Time, the hypocritic Days." Hypocritic is an odd word for a day. Emerson means they wear a mask. A day looks plain, quiet, one more Tuesday, and hides what it's carrying. Second, the offer. "To each they offer gifts after his will, Bread, kingdoms, stars, and sky that holds them all." Look at the range. Bread at one end, the whole sky at the other. Each day, the poem says, offers whatever you're willing to ask for, from the smallest need to the largest wonder. Third, what he took. The man in the garden forgets what he wished for that morning. He reaches out, and he "Took a few herbs and apples, and the Day Turned and departed silent." A few herbs. Not wrong, not wicked, just small. He took less than was offered, out of hurry or habit. Then, too late, the poem says, he saw the Day's scorn under her solemn headband. Fourth, what's new here. Earlier on this path, in an essay, Emerson pictured the days as veiled figures bearing gifts. In the poem, the blame turns on the watcher: he forgot his morning wishes. It isn't a poem about doing more. Herbs and apples are good things. It's about noticing what's being held out, and asking for something real. A conversation instead of a scroll. An hour outside instead of one more errand. The gift is already there. The poem's fear is only that we'll take the herbs out of habit.
screen: `THE DAYS WEAR A MASK.` · `BREAD, KINGDOMS, STARS, AND SKY.` · `HE TOOK A FEW HERBS.` · `NOTICE WHAT'S HELD OUT.` · then, large: `THE DAYS BRING GIFTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your morning wishes. Settle, and breathe. The man in the poem forgot what he had wished for that morning. Go back to the start of your own day, or to the last quiet moment you had. Was there a wish in it? To call someone. To be outside for an hour. To make something, or finish something, or rest. Let one forgotten wish come back. Then ask what today could hand you toward it, if you asked for more than herbs. Hold that one real gift. The bell holds the time.
Days. Emerson's short poem in which the days pass like silent, masked gift-bearers, and a man in his garden takes only a few herbs and apples. Today's word.
Your line: the days bring gifts. Today, ask the day for the one real gift you remembered, before it turns and goes. Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Days is a short poem often read aloud or memorized by readers of Emerson, as a reminder to notice what each ordinary day offers.

fork.setup: you're the man in the garden. a silent Day stops in front of you, holding out bread, kingdoms, stars and sky. you've forgotten your morning wishes. what does the poem say you do?
options: take a few herbs and apples.
fork.reveal: he hastily takes a few herbs and apples, and the Day turns and leaves. too late, he sees her scorn.

trapdoor: what you thought: Days is a sweet poem about enjoying life.
what it means: it's a warning dressed as a picture: each day offers gifts, and the speaker takes only a few herbs out of hurry.
what a scholar hears: Emerson calls the days hypocritic, meaning masked, and ends with the Day's scorn seen too late, under her solemn fillet.

notes: Editor pass: day 1209 already used Emerson's prose picture of the days as veiled gift-bearers (and a fork and practice built on it), so the teach now names that link and turns on what is new here, the forgotten morning wishes and the scorn seen too late; the practice now recalls a forgotten wish instead of repeating 1209's 'look for one gift'; cut the speculative 'a man who knew the days would not go on forever'.
